summary:
Moquegua department stands under Peru's national framework: the country does not criminalise trans identity, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising. No Moquegua-specific trans law, ordinance, court finding or enforcement action appears in the sources, and the national rules bind the department.

Two legislative stages govern restroom access. On 20 February 2025 the Congress' Commission on Women and Family unanimously approved a dictamen covering bills 6506 and 8457, which would bar entry to public sanitary facilities designated for the sex other than one's birth sex, with exceptions only for custody, medical care, or accompanying an adult, a child under 12 or a disabled person, and would require unambiguous signage; as of publication the measure still awaited plenary backing. The plenary approved the text on 2 April 2025, exempt from a second vote, as article 5 of the law 'fortaleciendo el derecho a la indemnidad sexual de los niños y adolescentes', which bars anyone whose biological sex does not match the facility's intended sex from public sanitary facilities, with exceptions limited to accompanying or assisting minors, patients or people with specific needs. A trans visitor to Moquegua should expect refusal of entry to a facility that matches their gender identity.

Trans-rights activist Gianna Camacho warned that the practical effect is that security staff would judge individuals by personal criteria, such as demanding the DNI. The restriction reaches private premises as well as public buildings: a consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy.

The Pontifical Catholic University of Peru's human-rights institute IDEHPUCP, in an analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte published on 15 April 2025, finds that article 5 implicitly brands trans people as more prone to entering bathrooms in order to harass or sexually abuse minors, conditions basic rights on a verifiable 'biological sex', and violates equality, non-discrimination and gender self-determination. The same analysis records that Congress had already banned inclusive language and again rejected equal marriage, and IDEHPUCP has documented dehumanising comparisons made on the congressional floor by congressman Lizarzaburu.

Violence risk is documented and under-counted. The TLGBI Rights Observatory's annual report records 54 killings of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases in Peru between 2020 and 2023, trans women the most affected and hate crimes rising; co-author Gianna Camacho, a trans journalist and human-rights defender, states that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry. One case from February 2023 illustrates the pattern: trans woman Rubí Torres Silvano, aged 31, was kidnapped in central Lima and murdered in Carabayllo with around 30 gunshots by the 'Los Gallegos' gang, the bodies showing gunshots, stab wounds and throat-slitting that indicate extreme hate. In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack: Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the regional human rights court's first torture-by-discrimination case.

Two protective findings sit alongside these risks. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings, and in July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.
tangentialFactors:
Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. The outcome leaves Peru one of only three South American countries, alongside Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

The April 2025 law's reach extends beyond facilities. Vague child-protection articles, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years. Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people. The same legislative package bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'.

Hostility is expressed publicly as well as legally. On television, presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'. The bathroom policy's extension into private life is illustrated by Lima, where a consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's complaint against a gym; Lima is a single data point, but it indicates how the national rule is applied in commercial settings that would also operate in Moquegua.
localsOnly:
Residents of Moquegua are governed by article 5 of the April 2025 law, which ties access to every public restroom to biological sex and confines exceptions to accompanying or assisting minors, patients or people with specific needs. Verification rests with security staff, who may demand a DNI, so the practical test is applied by individuals rather than by a defined procedure.

Since the 2017 repeal, residents have no hate-crime or anti-discrimination coverage for LGBT people in the Penal Code, which removes a formal route of protection after acts motivated by sexual orientation or gender identity. Recorded cases between 2020 and 2023 number 54 killings and 170 rights-violation cases nationally, trans women most affected, and those totals are described by their co-author as a sub-registry.

Healthcare and civic life carry their own rules. Inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity' is banned, inclusive language has been prohibited in Congress, and official health guidance no longer pathologises gender diversity after the June 2024 revision, which improves the terms on which trans patients are treated. Minimum sentences for obscenity rose from three to four years under the April 2025 law.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source records a Moquegua-specific enforcement action, municipal ordinance, police practice or hate-crime incident in the department; whether article 5 has been applied to a trans person in Moquegua is not sourced.

The February 2025 and April 2025 reports describe successive stages of the same legislative package, from committee approval awaiting plenary backing to plenary approval on 2 April 2025. Whether any constitutional challenge to article 5 has been filed or decided is unresolved in the inventory.

Statistics on killings and rights violations are national, with no breakdown for Moquegua or for any department; the proportion of cases occurring in the department is not sourced.

Whether the consumer-protection body's dismissal of the gym complaint or the on-air harassment of Susel Paredes produced any sanction, appeal or further proceeding is unresolved.

The sources do not state whether the June 2024 health-guidance revision or the July 2025 constitutional court ruling has been implemented in Moquegua's health services or courts.
